en: The *Prajñāpāramitā-rakṣā-ṣoḍaśa-bhadra-devaputra-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrajñāna:
The benevolent deity Dhataraṭṭha is greenish-blue in color. His mouth is open, manifesting a wrathful appearance.
Clad in armor and wearing crimson robes,
he holds a great sword in his right hand and cradles a spear in his left.
The hair is purple.
The benevolent deity Vairocana is crimson-purple in color;
he manifests a wrathful aspect with his lips tightly compressed.
The right hand brandishes a vajra;
the left rests upon the waist.
He is clad in armor and wears garments of white and blue.
His hair and beard are deep blue-black.
He subdues and overcomes malevolent spirits. His beard stands upright like a *miya* [mountain peak].
His flesh is the color of vermilion.
The right hand holds a great sword;
the left hand is extended outward at the chest.
He is clad in armor and wears white garments; the rest is as usual.
The deity who increases merit is flesh-colored red.
He has four arms and a wrathful countenance.
His first right hand holds a great sword.
The second hand holds a sword-wheel;
the first left hand holds a willow branch,
and the second left hand cradles a crescent moon.
He wears a kaṣāya of green color;
his lower garment is red, and he has a necklace suspended from his neck.
The deity Harṣa is green in color.
Above his head is a peacock,
golden in color;
in his right hand he holds a single-pronged hook.
His left hand rests upon his waist;
he is clad in armor and wears crimson robes,
with his hair and beard dyed a vermilion color.
The essence of the face is wrathful.
He is a benevolent deity who removes all obstacles and difficulties;
he is yellow in color and displays a wrathful expression.
Six-armed and clad in fresh white garments,
his right hand holds a trident,
and his next hand holds a scripture.
Next, he holds a precious stūpa containing śarīra relics in his hands;
his left hand holds a red lotus flower,
and his next hand holds a jeweled hook.
Next, holding a precious conch in his hand,
wearing a jeweled crown and a *kāṣāya*,
he blows upon the wind of celestial garments.
His necklaces, bracelets, and armlets are as usual.
The benevolent deity who eradicates the defilements of sin is naked, yet wears a saffron-colored robe;
his hair and body hair stand erect.
He has a reddish-yellow appearance.
His right hand holds a staff,
and that staff has five prongs.
The left hand forms a fist placed upon the crown of the head;
with eyes glaring and mouth agape,
sharp fangs protrude from both the upper and lower jaws.
It is most terrifying.
The benevolent deity Nairṛti has a void-colored body;
in his right hand, he holds a great sword.
In his left hand he holds a spear;
he wears a turban on his head,
which is white in color and reaches down to his kneecaps, where only the tip of its hem is visible.
His hair and beard are purple; he stands on the right side above.
The benevolent deity Vaiśravaṇa is dark blue-black in color and manifests the appearance of a wrathful king.
He forms the gesture of closed lips;
his right hand holds a vajra staff,
and his left hand cradles a precious stupa containing the entire body relics.
Clad in armor and wearing red garments,
with purple hair and beard;
the yakṣa Virūpākṣa is the color of flesh.
A black silk armlet is suspended [from the shoulder],
with a brush held in the posture of writing;
he is clad in armor and wears green garments.
The hair on his temples and his locks are red;
he has a smiling countenance.
The deity who is free from all fear has a physical form like that of Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
On his crown there is a skull,
and upon the skull is a trident-shaped emblem.
He is the Protector of All Beings, a benevolent deity of bluish-white color.
His appearance is like that of Vaiśravaṇa;
his left and right hands are joined in *añjali*,
and at the tips of his ten fingers are slightly blooming red lotuses.
His garments are reddish-yellow;
he subdues all demons and benevolent deities; his hair and body hairs stand erect;
his flesh is black in color.
His appearance is adorned with necklaces;
his right hand holds a sword,
and the palm of his left hand faces outward.
His robes are yellow.
He is a benevolent deity capable of saving all beings. His complexion is white and green, with features as beautiful as jade.
With both hands joined in the hollowed *añjali* gesture, he bends his two index fingers.
Attached to the first joint on the back of the middle finger:
he wears a white *kāṣāya* over his breast,
and his lower garment is red.
The deity Siṃhavikrama is of a flesh-colored complexion and wears a jeweled crown adorned with a lion.
His first right hand holds an axe;
his second right hand holds a sword.
The first left hand holds a *pustaka* (scripture);
the second left hand holds a trident.
He is clad in a *kāṣāya* robe of deep blue color.
Clad in a small garment of tiger skin,
he is extremely fierce and wrathful.
A benevolent deity with a courageous mind, he is armored in green.
If he is to rescue those in the realms of existence,
his two hands are bound externally at the chest in the gesture of smiling;
he is thus depicted standing on the left side.
The original colophon states:
Furthermore, the third fascicle of the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha-sūtra* sets forth the names of the sixteen benevolent deities along with their collective mantra.
It is also as described above regarding the dream-vision experienced by the Bhikṣu Kōng, in which he was inspired by the Vinaya Master of his own stūpa courtyard.
The *Guxiang ji* (Collection of Echoes from the Valleys), fascicle eight, states:
"In the world there is a work in one scroll and three sheets titled *Shanbao jingangzhi yifu shiliu shanshen* (Sixteen Benevolent Deities for the Protection of Prajñā Translated by Vajrabodhi).
Upon reading it, it is clearly evident that these words were not penned by Vajrabodhi."
My composition is extremely clumsy.
I imagine that the former masters, relying on the diagrams of Vajrabodhi,
recorded them and attributed the name "Vajra-wisdom" to this work as a courtesy.
I am truly unaware of my own extreme limitations.
Now, it is said that at the translation assembly, there shall be established positions such as the oral interpreter (*yanyu*), the scribe (*bishou*), the verifier of meaning (*zhengyi*),
and the editor (*zhuwen*) to translate from Sanskrit into Chinese.
It is certainly not the work of a single hand by the original translator;
some parts have been revised while others have not,
with the sole aim of ensuring the meaning is fully communicated as its primary merit.
How could this be considered mere literary embellishment?
This year, I obtained a copy from the Abbot’s quarters of Chijikyū-in;
having compared it with the copy held in the Shōchihō-bō collection, I have printed and circulated it.
Recorded by the śramaṇa Kaidō of Ryūge on Mount Hōzan during the middle month of summer in the second year of the Enpō era (1674).
Proofread once by Jishun.
On the final day of the second month of autumn in the third year of Bunka (the Gengchen year),
the right-hand portion was also completed after being collated once more against the copy prepared by the Śrāmaṇera Shuyō Ryūmitsu.
Dragon liver.
